usage: '키우다' (to raise/rear) is the natural verb for having a pet, never '가지다' (to possess)
the particle '과/와' frames the dog as your companion on the walk, not an object you take
'동반(同伴)' = accompanying together; a fixed sign-word you see at pet-friendly venues
Koreans say '우리(our)' even for a personal pet, the same warm 'our' used in '우리 집, 우리 엄마'
examples: 저는 강아지 한 마리를 키워요.
I raise one dog.
everyday speech drops '반려견' for plain '강아지'; animals are counted with '마리'

This cafe allows companion dogs.

Registering your companion dog is a legally set obligation.
real-life: micro-chipping/registering a dog is mandatory in Korea, so this exact phrasing appears on official notices
nuance: '반려견(伴侶犬)' is the warm, modern word for a pet dog, built from the hanja 반려(伴侶) 'companion/life-partner' + 견(犬) 'dog' — literally 'companion dog,' the very same 반려 used in 반려자 'one's spouse.' It has deliberately replaced the older near-synonym '애완견(愛玩犬),' where 애완(愛玩) means 'love-and-play-with,' i.e. treat as a cherished toy; the dividing line is respect — '애완견' frames the dog as a possession, '반려견' as family, so '애완견' now sounds dated and faintly callous in public or official use. Register-wise '반려견' is the polite/written form you use at vets, in signs, and in news; in casual chat Koreans almost always just say '강아지' regardless of the dog's age. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for '가지다(to have/own)' — you do not 'have' a dog in Korean, you 키우다 'raise' it, and you say 우리 강아지 'our dog' even when it is solely yours.

nuance: '반려묘(伴侶猫)' pairs the hanja 반려(伴侶 'companion') with 묘(猫 'cat') and is the formal/written counterpart to '반려견,' carrying the same respectful 'family member' nuance; you meet it at vet clinics, pet shops, and on official notices. Its dated near-synonym is '애완묘(愛玩猫),' which (like '애완견') frames the cat as a plaything and now sounds cold — the dividing line is exactly the same respect gradient as 반려/애완. The key register fact English speakers miss: '반려묘' is essentially never used in everyday conversation, where '고양이' is the only natural word — saying '반려묘' to a friend sounds like you are reading a poster. nuance: '사료(飼料)' joins the hanja 사(飼 'to feed/rear') and 료(料 'material/stuff') — literally 'feeding-material' — and is the standard word for processed pet food, covering both dry kibble and wet pouches, as well as livestock feed; context alone tells you whether it's a cat or a cow. The crucial near-synonym contrast is '사료' vs '간식(間食)': '사료' is the daily staple meal, while '간식' (lit. 'between-meals food') is treats/snacks — calling a treat '사료' sounds wrong to a Korean ear. Another boundary is '사료' vs '음식(飮食)': '음식' is food for people, so using it for an animal's meal is a직역 trap; animals eat '사료,' people eat '음식.' Register is neutral and everyday. usage: '하다' is the casual, all-purpose verb for putting a leash on
'채우다(to fasten/buckle)' is more precise than '하다' — it pictures the clasp closing
'풀다(to undo/release)' is the natural opposite of 채우다
'착용(着用) 필수' = wearing-is-mandatory — the fixed phrasing on park signs
examples: 우리 강아지는 목줄을 싫어해요.
My dog hates the leash.
simple level: '싫어하다' = to dislike; topic '목줄을' takes object 을
밖에 나갈 때는 꼭 목줄을 채워야 해요.
When going outside you must fasten the leash.
everyday rule: '-아야 해요' = have to; '채우다' is the natural verb for buckling it on
공원에서는 목줄을 풀면 안 돼요.
In the park you can't let your dog off-leash.
real-life: leashing in public is law in Korea; '-면 안 되다' = must not
nuance: '목줄' is a pure-Korean compound of 목 'neck' + 줄 'rope/cord,' literally 'neck-rope,' and in everyday speech it loosely covers both the collar and the walking leash. The sharp near-synonym distinctions matter: the long walking line alone is often '리드줄' or just '줄'; a body harness worn across the chest (not the neck) is a completely different word, '하네스' or '가슴줄(chest-strap),' so calling a harness '목줄' is wrong. Also avoid the generic '끈(string/cord)' for a pet leash — '끈' is shoelace-level string, '목줄' is the specific pet item. The verb pair to lock in is 채우다(fasten on) ↔ 풀다(take off); '하다' works casually but '채우다/풀다' sound more native. Register is neutral and practical: because leashing in public is the law, the sign-phrase '목줄 착용 필수' is everywhere, and the English-speaker pitfall is saying '목줄을 입다(wear)' — clothing uses 입다, but a leash/collar is 채우다 or 하다.

usage: '하다' here means to carry out / receive the shot
'맞다(to be struck by)' is the idiomatic verb for getting any injection
'기록(記錄 record)' — vets keep one that boarding/grooming places ask for
'정기(定期 fixed-period)' = regular/scheduled, vs a one-off shot
examples: 오늘 강아지가 주사를 맞았어요.
Today my dog got a shot.
simple level: casual '주사(shot)' + '맞다'; the animal itself is the subject receiving it
광견병 예방접종은 매년 맞혀야 해요.
The rabies vaccination has to be given every year.
everyday: '광견병(狂犬病)' = rabies; '맞히다' is the causative — you have your pet get it
입소 전에 예방접종 기록을 보여 주세요.
Please show the vaccination record before check-in.
real-life: boarding facilities and groomers require this before admission
nuance: '예방접종(豫防接種)' stacks the hanja 예방(豫防 'prevent in advance') + 접종(接種 'graft/inoculate'), literally 'preventive inoculation,' and is the full, mildly formal clinic term; in casual speech people shorten it to '접종' or just say '주사(注射 injection/shot).' The near-synonym line is scope: '예방접종' specifically means a preventive vaccine, whereas '주사' is any shot at all (including treatment injections), so they overlap but aren't identical. The signature English-speaker pitfall is the verb pair 맞다 vs 맞히다: '맞다' literally 'to be struck' is how Korean says 'receive an injection,' so the pet 주사를 맞다; when YOU take the pet to get the shot, you use the causative '맞히다' — 강아지에게 주사를 맞히다 'have the dog get a shot.' A second trap is the English instinct to 'take/get' or even 'eat' a vaccine: in Korean a shot is 맞다(received by needle), never 먹다(eat) — '백신을 먹다' is only correct for an oral vaccine, which is rare. Rabies (광견병) vaccination is legally mandatory and renewed yearly in Korea, so '매년 맞히다' is common.

usage: almost always paired with '수술(手術 surgery)' — the complete, natural form
'하다' for having the procedure done in general terms
'시키다' makes it causative (written solid) — you arrange it for the pet

examples: 우리 고양이는 중성화를 했어요.
Our cat has been neutered.
simple level: '중성화를 하다' as the basic done-state
보호소에서 중성화 수술을 한 뒤에 입양 보내요.
The shelter neuters them before adopting them out.
everyday: '-ㄴ 뒤에' = after; '입양 보내다' = rehome
중성화를 하면 성격이 차분해진다고 해요.
They say neutering makes them calmer.
real-life hearsay: '-다고 해요' = it is said that; '차분해지다' = become calm
nuance: '중성화(中性化)' is built from 중성(中性 'neutral/neuter gender,' the same 중성 used in chemistry for 'neutral') + 화(化 '-ization/turning into'), so it literally means 'turning gender-neutral' and serves as the single umbrella term for both spaying females and neutering males — unlike English, everyday Korean does not split the two into separate words. It is almost always spoken as the fuller '중성화 수술(neutering surgery)'; bare '중성화' alone can sound clipped. A useful contrast: '중성화' is the elective desexing procedure, distinct from '불임(不姙 infertility),' which describes the resulting inability to reproduce, not the operation. The causative '중성화시키다' or '중성화를 하다' both work because the owner arranges what is done to the pet. Register is neutral-clinical; shelters and street-cat TNR (포획-중성화-방사) programs use this exact word, and 'TNR' itself is widely understood. The English-speaker pitfall is hunting for gendered terms like a 'spay' word — there isn't one; '중성화' covers both sexes, and dropping '수술' is the other common slip.

usage: the general verb for adopting in (receiving) a pet or child
'보내다(to send off)' marks the giving side — you send the animal to a new home
common cause-driven collocation pairing 유기견 + 입양
Korea's well-known animal-welfare slogan; '사지 말고' = don't buy, instead...
examples: 저는 고양이를 입양했어요.
I adopted a cat.
simple level: '입양하다' with the cat as object 을
사지 말고 입양하세요.
Adopt, don't shop.
everyday slogan: the famous '사지 말고 입양하세요' on posters and campaigns
새끼 고양이를 입양 보낼 곳을 찾고 있어요.
I'm looking for a home to adopt out the kittens.
real-life: '입양 보낼 곳' = a place to send them; note the giving direction 보내다
nuance: '입양(入養)' combines the hanja 입(入 'enter') + 양(養 'rear/nurture'), literally 'enter-to-be-raised,' and is the very same word used for adopting a child — applying it to pets deliberately signals the modern view that an animal joins the family rather than being purchased like goods. The decisive contrast for learners is direction, encoded by the helper verbs: '입양하다' (or 입양을 받다) means to adopt IN, i.e. you receive the pet, while '입양 보내다' means to adopt OUT, i.e. you give a pet away to a new home — same noun 입양, opposite flow set by 하다/받다 versus 보내다, and mixing these reverses your meaning. The other near-synonym tension is '입양하다' vs '사다(buy)': both can get you a pet, but '사다' frames it as a commercial transaction, which is exactly what the slogan '사지 말고 입양하세요(adopt, don't shop)' rejects; for shelter animals '입양' is the warmer, socially endorsed verb. Register is neutral and widely positive. The English pitfall is assuming 'adopt' is one-directional — in Korean you must pick the right helper to show whether the pet is coming to you or leaving you.

mistakes: Confusing direction: '입양하다' is RECEIVING a pet, '입양 보내다' is GIVING one away — the helper verb (하다/받다 vs 보내다) flips the meaning
Using '사다(buy)' for a shelter pet: it sounds like a purchase; '입양하다' is the kinder, expected verb (hence '사지 말고 입양하세요')
Saying '입양을 가다(go to adopt)' to mean you adopted — to receive a pet, the verb is '입양하다/입양을 받다', not 가다

usage: '구조하다(救助 to rescue)' — the verb for saving an animal in distress
'보호소(保護所 protection-place)' where rescued dogs are kept
frequently paired collocation; adopting an ex-stray carries positive weight
'출신(出身 originating from)' describes a dog's background, like 'graduated from'
examples: 우리 강아지는 유기견이었어요.
Our dog used to be a stray.
simple level: '-이었어요' past tense for a former state ('was a...')
저는 유기견 보호소에서 봉사활동을 해요.
I volunteer at an abandoned-dog shelter.
everyday: '봉사활동(volunteer work)' is a very common collocation with 하다
길에서 유기견을 발견하면 신고하세요.
If you find a stray dog, report it.
real-life: '발견하다' = discover/find; you can report to a shelter or a city hotline
nuance: '유기견(遺棄犬)' is built from 유기(遺棄 'to abandon/desert,' the same 유기 in legal '유기죄 abandonment crime') + 견(犬 'dog'), so it specifically means a dog DESERTED BY ITS OWNER — a former pet now without a home. This is its key contrast with near-synonyms: '들개' is a feral/wild dog born and living on the streets (never owned), while '길고양이(street cat)' is the gentle everyday term for community cats; so '유기견' carries the extra meaning of betrayal/abandonment that '들개' lacks. The exact cat counterpart is '유기묘.' A spelling-look-alike pitfall for learners: the prefix 유기- here is 遺棄 'abandon' and is completely unrelated to '유기농(有機農 organic farming),' where 유기 is 有機 'organic' — same sound, different hanja, opposite topic. Register is neutral and the word appears constantly in animal-welfare contexts; adopting a '유기견' is socially praised in Korea, so phrases like '유기견 출신' (ex-stray background) are said with warmth, not stigma. The English-speaker trap is flattening 'stray' onto every loose dog — reserve '유기견' for abandoned ex-pets, not truly wild '들개.'

mistakes: Confusing '유기견(abandoned by an owner)' with '들개(a truly feral dog born wild)' — 유기견 implies a former pet that was deserted
Misreading the 유기- prefix: it is 遺棄 'abandoned', NOT 有機 'organic' as in '유기농' — same sound, unrelated meaning
Using '유기견' for a stray cat — the cat words are '유기묘' (formal) or '길고양이' (everyday)

usage: '깎다(to clip/shave off)' — the grooming verb for cutting them down
'갈다(to grind/file)' — what a cat does on a scratcher, not what you do with clippers
the cue that it's time for a trim; '길다' = to be long
one word from 깎다 + -이 (the tool suffix); compare '손톱깎이' for human nails
examples: 고양이 발톱이 길어요.
The cat's claws are long.
simple level: descriptive '길다'; the cue to trim
강아지 발톱을 직접 깎아 줘요.
I trim my dog's nails myself.
everyday: '직접' = personally; '깎아 주다' = trim it (for the dog's benefit)
고양이가 자꾸 소파에 발톱을 갈아요.
The cat keeps sharpening its claws on the sofa.
real-life: '자꾸' = repeatedly; why scratching posts ('스크래처') exist — note 갈다, not 깎다
nuance: '발톱' is a pure-Korean compound of 발 'foot/paw' + 톱 'saw/serrated edge,' covering both a human's toenail and an animal's foot-claw with context deciding which. Its essential paired contrast is the body part '손톱' (손 'hand' + 톱) = fingernail/hand-claw versus '발톱' = the foot/paw nail; an animal walking on all fours has 발톱 on every paw, so calling them '손톱' is wrong. The trickier learner trap is the two grooming verbs that both attach to 발톱: '깎다' means YOU trim/clip them with clippers (a grooming act of removal), whereas '갈다' means the cat sharpens/grinds them on a surface (the cat's own act) — same noun, opposite agents and actions, so '발톱을 깎다' = you cut them, '발톱을 갈다' = the cat files them. Note also '갈다' is a homonym: here 'grind/sharpen,' but elsewhere 'replace' (배변패드를 갈다) — context separates them. Register is neutral everyday. Overgrown 발톱 can curl into the paw, so '발톱이 길면 다칠 수 있어요' is a common care reminder.

mistakes: Using '손톱(fingernail/hand-claw)' for an animal's paw claws — paws take '발톱' (발 'foot' + 톱)
Mixing up '깎다(you clip/trim them)' with '갈다(the cat sharpens/grinds them)' — different agents and actions on the same 발톱
Forgetting '갈다' is a homonym: 'sharpen' here but 'replace' elsewhere; let context (claws vs a pad) decide the meaning

usage: the noun takes '하다' to become the verb 'go through shedding'
'철' = (natural) season; spring and fall are the heavy ones
'심하다(to be severe/intense)' is the natural partner for heavy shedding
'시기(時期 period/time)' — interchangeable with '철' but slightly more neutral
examples: 요즘 털이 많이 빠져요.
Lately a lot of hair is falling out.
simple level: '털이 빠지다' = hair falls out, the observable sign of shedding
털갈이할 때는 빗질을 자주 해 주세요.
During shedding, brush often.
everyday care: '빗질' = brushing/combing; '-할 때' = when/during
우리 고양이는 봄가을마다 털갈이가 정말 심해요.
My cat sheds really heavily every spring and fall.
real-life: '-마다' = every; long-haired breeds shed a lot seasonally
nuance: '털갈이' is a pure-Korean compound of 털 'fur/hair' + 갈이 (from 갈다 'to replace/change,' nominalized), literally 'fur-changing,' and names the seasonal coat turnover when a pet sheds its old fur for a new layer; it peaks in spring and autumn, hence the common '봄/가을 털갈이 철.' The sharp near-synonym contrast learners need is '털갈이' vs '탈모(脫毛)': '털갈이' is the normal, healthy seasonal shed, whereas '탈모' (hanja 脫 'come off' + 毛 'hair') is hair LOSS/balding that signals a problem (illness, stress, skin disease) — so describing routine seasonal shedding as '탈모' wrongly implies your pet is sick. A grammar pitfall is the verb: because '갈이' already carries the 갈다 root as a fixed noun, you say '털갈이를 하다,' not '털을 갈다'; the compound is frozen. Also distinguish the everyday observation '털이 빠지다(hair falls out)' — that describes the symptom, while '털갈이' names the whole seasonal event. Register is neutral and conversational among pet owners, who reach for a '빗(brush)' and do extra '빗질' to manage the loose '빠진 털' during this period.

usage: the basic phrase; the destination takes '에' (location of arrival)
'데려가다(take a living being along)' — essential for animals/people
'가깝다(near)' modifying it — useful when searching a map app
'24시(twenty-four-hour)' = open around the clock, for emergencies
examples: 근처에 동물병원이 있어요?
Is there a vet clinic nearby?
simple level: existence question '있어요?' — handy for a new resident
고양이가 아파서 동물병원에 데려갔어요.
My cat was sick so I took it to the vet.
everyday: cause '-아서'; '데려가다' for living things, not '가져가다'
밤에 응급 상황이면 24시 동물병원을 찾으세요.
If it's an emergency at night, find a 24-hour vet.
real-life: '응급 상황' = emergency situation; '찾다' = look for/find
nuance: '동물병원(動物病院)' is transparently 동물(動物 'animal') + 병원(病院 'hospital,' itself 병 'illness' + 원 'institution'), literally 'animal hospital,' and is the one standard word for any vet clinic, large or small — there is no separate casual term, so you use it with friends and on signs alike. Don't confuse the place with the person: '수의사(獸醫師 'beast-doctor')' is the veterinarian, while '동물병원' is where they work — so '수의사 병원' is not how Koreans name the clinic. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the take-verb: Korean strictly separates '데려가다' (take/bring a LIVING being along) from '가져가다' (carry an OBJECT), so you 강아지를 동물병원에 데려가다 — using '가져가다' for your pet treats it like luggage and sounds jarring (the same 데리다/가지다 split applies to people: you 데려가다 a friend, never 가져가다). Register is neutral. For overnight crises, larger cities have '24시 동물병원,' and the location particle is '에' (동물병원에 가다/데려가다).

Calling the clinic '수의사 병원': the place is '동물병원'; '수의사(獸醫師)' is the vet, the person who works there

usage: '깔다(to spread/lay out flat)' — putting a fresh pad on the floor
'갈다(to replace)' — swapping out a soiled pad for a new one
'훈련(訓練 training)' — teaching a puppy to go on the pad
have an accident off the pad
'실수하다(to make a mistake)' — i.e. the dog goes in the wrong spot
examples: 강아지가 배변패드에 잘 싸요.
The dog goes nicely on the pee pad.
simple level: '싸다' = to relieve oneself — casual but standard for pets; location takes 에
배변패드를 매일 갈아 줘야 해요.
You have to change the pee pad every day.
everyday: '갈아 주다' = change it (for the pet's benefit); '-아야 하다' = have to
아직 배변패드 훈련이 안 됐어요.
It's not potty-pad trained yet.
real-life: '훈련이 되다' = to be/get trained; '아직 안 됐다' = not done yet
nuance: '배변패드' is a hybrid word: the Sino-Korean 배변(排便 'discharge-feces,' from 배 排 'expel' + 변 便 'excrement') plus the English loanword 패드(pad), literally 'elimination pad,' and it is the standard product name for the absorbent floor pads apartment-dwelling dog owners rely on indoors. The two verbs that pair with it must not be swapped: '깔다' = lay out a FRESH pad (spread it flat on the floor), while '갈다' = REPLACE a used one (the same 갈다 'replace' seen in 털갈이 and 사료를 갈다) — they name different steps in the routine, so '깔다' is setup and '갈다' is the daily swap. A meaning-boundary pitfall: don't say '기저귀(diaper),' which is worn ON the body — the floor product is '배변패드'; a wearable pet diaper would be '강아지 기저귀,' a different item. Register is everyday and practical. Because most Koreans live in apartments without yards, indoor '배변패드 훈련' is extremely common rather than relying on outdoor walks alone, and the blunt-but-normal pet verb '싸다(relieve itself)' is used freely here without sounding crude.
